description:
*GOD'S PRESENCE*
*Sermon Summary*

This sermon centers on the idea that what truly makes a home, a church, or a blessed life is not the physical structure or religious activity, but the Presence of God.
We began by acknowledging that many people come from broken or unhappy homes and urges the church to care for one another’s families rather than judge them. Just as people make a house a home by inhabiting it, God’s Presence is what makes a life or church spiritually alive.

Using the story of the Ark of the Covenant, we explained that wherever God’s Presence went, there was victory, breakthrough, and blessing - except when Israel treated it as a religious object or a transactional tool. This leads to the main point: obedience to God is not a transaction to “pay” for blessings. God has already blessed believers with spiritual blessings, but obedience keeps them in right relationship with Him so His Presence remains active in their lives.

Without God’s Presence, religious actions are empty. With His Presence, believers can face any challenge with confidence. The sermon concludes by applying this principle to practical areas - especially finances and tithing - saying that obedience in areas where one needs breakthrough invites God’s Presence into that area, leading to real change. Ultimately, the message is that obedience is about relationship, not bargaining, and that God’s Presence is the key to blessing, protection, and victory.

title: God Uses The Unlikely
description:
*GOD USES UNLIKELY PEOPLE*
*Sermon Summary*

Using the story of Gideon in Judges, we saw how God intentionally reduced Gideon’s army from thousands to just 300 men. Even more surprising, God chose the men who appeared less dignified - the ones who drank water like dogs - rather than those who seemed more proper. The point is that victory didn’t come through human strength, strategy, or impressiveness, but through God’s power. When the odds are stacked against us and things move in the opposite direction of what makes sense, it may not be failure or attack - it may be God positioning Himself to receive the glory.
We see this in the testimony of our church. The growth and victories are not due to talent, experience, long years in church, or polished leadership. The church’s progress is clearly God’s Work - not human brilliance.
We highlighted ordinary members - people serving in practical, unseen ways as evidence that God builds His Kingdom through willing, imperfect people. The culture of humility, sacrifice, and making room for others reflects a community shaped by grace rather than status.

The message then becomes personal: your past mistakes, failures, and brokenness may actually be the reason God can use you. If you had it all together, people might credit you. But when someone who was once lost, messy, or struggling is transformed, others see that it had to be Jesus. Your testimony becomes powerful precisely because you were unlikely.

We connected this to faith (Hebrews 11:1), describing faith as “evidence” that produces conviction even when there is no visible proof. Faith paints a picture in your heart before circumstances change. Even when others doubt, mock, or don’t understand, faith holds onto what God can do.

The sermon closes with a call to embrace being part of the “unlikely” group - people who don’t appear impressive, qualified, or polished, but who trust a great God. Throughout Scripture, it is often the confident, self-assured people who fall, while the humble and dependent are used mightily. The victory, then, is never about the stone and sling, the army, or the leader - it’s about God.

You may feel unqualified, broken, or unlikely, but that may be exactly why God will use you. And when He does, everyone will know it was Him.

title: Audacious Faith (Part 2) l 18 January 2026 l Pastor Jeremy Govender
description:
We used a prop - a heavy weight to symbolize the burdens of life - illness, financial strain, broken relationships, and personal struggles. These challenges don’t negotiate or disappear just because we wish for easier circumstances. Wishing is not faith.

We then used two ropes:
One was a thick, strong rope that obviously can lift the weight.
One was a thin, unlikely rope that seems too weak.

The thick rope represents human effort - education, discipline, advice, and self-improvement. These are good and necessary, but they are not faith. If we can reach our goals through our own strength, it doesn’t require trusting God.

The thin rope represents true faith - believing God for what looks impossible. The reason we can trust Him is because we have His Word, the “fact sheet” that tells us what He is capable of. Faith comes by hearing the Word of God. Even mustard-seed faith is enough.

Many Christians claim to have faith but still rely on their own methods - using the thick rope when God is asking them to trust Him. Like a football team that receives a winning game plan from the head coach but continues to play the old, losing way, believers often hear God’s Word on Sunday and then return to their old habits on Monday.

We were challenged to look at the impossible situation in our lives and face the simple question: Either God can, or God can’t. If you believe God can, then trust Him and obey what He says - run the play. Don’t depend on what “makes sense” to the world, like Saul’s armour. Be like David and use what God has given, trusting that He is enough.

The Message ended with a call to deepen faith, stand on Scripture, and believe boldly: Your God can.

title: What It Could Be l 25 December 2025 l Pastor Jeremy Govender
description:
Christmas joy is not sentiment or “magic”; it is the joy of Jesus entering a broken world and a broken life. The story of Bethlehem is tender and beautiful, but it is also gritty and real—Mary’s vulnerability, Joseph’s risk, doors closed in Bethlehem, danger from Herod, and yet heaven breaking in among ordinary people. That Child in a manger is not simply a reason for a holiday; He is the reason anyone can be saved. Christmas is the beginning of redemption. It is the light that runs through a Cross and an empty tomb, giving sinners a second birth and opening eternity.

Some smile while carrying quiet pain. Into that mix comes the question Jesus asked a man who had waited thirty-eight years by the pool of Bethesda: Do you want to be made whole? The longer trouble lasts, the easier it is to stop hoping. But hope can live again with a simple surrender: "Yes, Lord, I do." Jesus is not one more option in a long line; He is the Lord who doesn’t wait for stirred water. He speaks, and the lame stand.

“Give us this day our daily bread” is not just a line to recite - it is a way to live. As God fed Israel with manna for forty years, so Jesus, the Bread of Life, sustains usl through the wilderness of life. Grace arrives on time - enough for today, and tomorrow will have its own supply. So why not make every day like Christmas Day - waking up to the news that Jesus has entered the situation, that He walks with His people and will lead them all the way to promise?

Imagine what can be when Jesus is welcomed into every need: the One who conquered sin, death, and the grave can heal a body, restore a marriage, free an addict, and provide where there is lack. Strip away the trimmings and traditions if you must. Make it about only Jesus, and there is still a reason to celebrate. Because He is enough, and He changes everything.

title: The Little Things l 21 December 2025 l Pastor Jeremy Govender
description:
In a season thick with Christmas atmosphere - decorations, carols, heat and buzzing grass cutters - we stressed the importance of a different atmosphere - the Presence of God. We don’t sing just to sing; we’re building an environment where the King is welcomed, and where bondage breaks without an altar call because He is here.

Creation itself teaches it. God forms the environment before He fills it. Fish flourish in water, birds in air, lions in their territory. Put a shark on land and it’s harmless, but step into its water it becomes deadly. In the same way, we were made from God and for God. Stay in Him, and the enemy can’t reach you. But step into the enemy's atmosphere and suddenly you’re fighting on his terms. The prodigal had provision in the father’s house but starved when he left. The devil can’t touch you in God’s Presence, so he whispers you out - “just a little,” “just this once,” “it’s not that big.”

That’s why small things matter. A big complicated machine can fail because of a tiny cable. Many are on the brink of breakthrough but leak power through “little” compromises. Samson didn’t fall in a day, and it wasn’t “Delilah’s fault.” It started earlier - honey from a dead lion’s carcass - an erosion of the Nazirite vow. When we tolerate small contamination, we end up giving the world cause to boast over our God. Yet hope remains - “his hair began to grow again.” God’s mercy means your greatest victory can still come after your greatest failure. So in this season, choose your atmosphere. Guard the small gates. Stay where you were made to live - near God, among His people, in simple obedience. Let this be a good Christmas not because the enemy leaves you alone, but because you refuse to answer his call.

title: The Cure l 7 December 2025 l Pastor Jeremy Govender
description:
*THE CURE FOR SIN*

_Isaiah 53:1 - 6_

*Sermon Summary*

Today we spoke about a hard but hopeful truth: sin is like a sickness. A good doctor doesn’t just diagnose; he treats. In the same way, I refuse to gather us just to say, “We’ve all sinned.” We need to talk about how to get well.

Isaiah says Jesus was wounded for our transgressions and bruised for our iniquities. Transgressions are the outward acts; iniquity is the inner bent, twisted places that keep leaning us toward the same old patterns. I compared it to our screen system: my phone doesn’t talk to the screens directly; it sends a signal to a receiver that’s already set up to listen. Temptation works like that. God doesn’t tempt us, and the devil can’t make us sin - but the enemy studies us and knows our “receiver settings,” those triggers and habits we’ve allowed to stay tuned to the wrong signal.

The cure isn’t pretending to be better. Morphine can numb a cancer patient; it can’t heal them. Behaviour modification alone won’t change a crooked heart. We need to be reprogrammed - no longer conformed to the world, but transformed by the renewing of our minds. That happens as we spend more time with God than with the noise that shapes us, and as we intentionally feed what we want to live and starve what needs to die. 

I pressed this now because December exposes our weak spots: irresponsible spending, parties, “just this once” choices. Self-examination matters - like Holy Communion calls us to do - so that our New Year can be better than the old. By God’s grace we can say, “I’m done being remote-controlled by old triggers. I belong to Jesus.” Name the patterns. Avoid the rooms. Feed your spirit. And let the Spirit reprogram what you can’t fix by willpower alone.

title: Puppy Love l 23 November 2025 l Pastor Jeremy Govender
description:
In the story of the Canaanite woman, we are confronted with a deeply uncomfortable moment: Jesus, the embodiment of love and compassion, uses a word that offends, calling her a “dog.” This is not a moment to explain away or soften; it is a moment to feel the weight of offense, to recognize the pain of being an outsider, and to acknowledge the reality that sometimes, even in the presence of God’s people, we are hurt, ignored, or made to feel unworthy. The context of the time was one of deep animosity between Jews and Canaanites, and the language used reflected that brokenness. Yet, it is precisely in this place of desperation and offense that the Canaanite woman’s faith shines.

Desperation often drives us to Jesus. Most of us do not come to God when life is perfect; we come when we are overwhelmed, when our problems are bigger than we are, when we have nowhere else to turn. Like the Canaanite woman, we may find ourselves doing things we never thought we would—pushing through barriers, risking rejection, and seeking help from those who might not welcome us. Her story is a mirror for all who have ever felt ignored by God or by His people, for those who have prayed and seen others receive their miracle while their own prayers seem unanswered.

The pain of being overlooked or mistreated by the church or by fellow Christians is real. Many have left the church because of such wounds. Yet, the Canaanite woman’s response is not to walk away, but to kneel at Jesus’ feet. She persists, not because the people around her are kind, but because she knows that only Jesus can help her. Her faith is not in the disciples, not in the institution, but in Christ alone. Even when called a dog, she recognizes that in the house of Jesus, even the crumbs are enough to bring healing.

There is a subtle but profound shift in Jesus’ words. While the world may call us outcasts, Jesus’ use of the word “puppy” (kunarion) hints at belonging, at being cared for within the household. It does not erase the offense, but it reframes it: in God’s house, even those who feel like outsiders are under His care. The challenge is to keep coming to Jesus, to worship through the hurt, to persist in faith even when the body of Christ fails us. For it is in that place of humble, desperate worship that miracles happen.

title: Throwing Stones l 16 November 2025 l Pastor Jeremy Govender
description:
The story of the woman caught in adultery is one we’ve all heard, but sometimes its power is lost in familiarity. Today, I invite us to see ourselves in her place—not just as observers, but as those who know what it is to carry shame, regret, and secrets we hope never come to light. Each of us, no matter how we present ourselves, has moments and memories we’d rather keep hidden. The truth is, just because we haven’t been exposed doesn’t mean we’re innocent. We all have fallen short, and it’s easy to judge others while hoping no one ever judges us.

We live in a world, and sometimes even in a church, where it’s become a pastime to throw stones—through gossip, criticism, and self-righteousness. We cover our own flaws with spiritual perfume and act as if we’re better than others, forgetting that the ground is level at the foot of the cross. The pain of being exposed, of having our worst moments put on display, is something we all fear. Yet, Jesus stands between us and the stones, not denying our failures, but offering grace instead of condemnation.

When Jesus stooped to write on the ground, He reminded the accusers—and us—that He is the author of the law, the judge, and the giver of grace. He knows every detail of our story, and still, He chooses mercy. He doesn’t ignore our sin, but He doesn’t let it define us either. He calls us to go and sin no more, not because we are perfect, but because He has made a way for us to be free.

People may never let go of our past. They may continue to gossip, to remind us of our failures, to question our worthiness. But Jesus writes a new ending to our story. Our shame is not the final word—His grace is. When others try to put a full stop on our lives, God says, “I am your beginning and your end.” Our focus, then, is not on the stones others throw, but on the grace that lifts us up and calls us forward. We are all works in progress, and by His grace, we wake up each day, forgiven and free to pursue the life He has written for us.

title: Miracles Happen In The Middle l 9 November 2025 l Pastor Jeremy Govender
description:
We reflect on the transforming power of God’s grace and the reality that miracles often happen in the “middle”—in the messy, uncertain, and difficult seasons of our lives. We celebrated stories of real people in our community who have experienced profound change, not because they were perfect or had it all together, but because they kept showing up, trusting that God could do what they could not. Whether it’s overcoming addiction, surviving broken relationships, or wrestling with doubt and guilt, we are reminded that God is not finished with us yet. The journey may be long, and sometimes we find ourselves stuck in patterns or circumstances that seem impossible to break. But God specializes in meeting us right there, in the middle of our struggle.

It’s easy to blame others or our circumstances for where we are. Many of us have legitimate reasons for our pain—family history, injustice, or wounds we never asked for. The world encourages us to stay in that place of blame, but God calls us to something more. The story of Israel’s journey to the Promised Land teaches us that while the giants in our lives are real and the obstacles are daunting, the crucial question is not just what stands against us, but whether we will trust God in the face of those giants. The first generation of Israelites missed out on God’s promise, not because the giants were too big, but because they chose not to believe that God could overcome them.

We see this pattern throughout Scripture: Noah, Joseph, Moses, Joshua—all faced impossible middles. The miracle was not just in the promise or the fulfillment, but in the faith to keep going when nothing seemed to change. Joshua and his people marched around Jericho day after day, seeing no results, but they kept going, believing that the next step could be the breakthrough. The call is to keep showing up, to keep trusting, to keep fighting—not against people, but against the spiritual forces that seek to keep us stuck. The victory is not won by those who never fall, but by those who refuse to forfeit, who keep stepping forward in faith, believing that God can and will do what He has promised.

title: Change the NAME, change the GAME l 2 November 2025 l Pastor Jeremy Govender
description:
The deeper truth is that God is at work in each of our lives, regardless of our past or present struggles. The story of Jacob, who was born with the name “deceiver” but was later called Israel, reminds us that our identity is not determined by our failures or the labels others place on us. Instead, God sees beyond our shortcomings and calls us to a greater purpose.

Jacob’s journey is a mirror for our own. Like him, we often find ourselves running from God, making choices that lead us away from His best, or simply trying to survive in a world that doesn’t always appreciate us. Yet, no matter how far we stray, something within us—God’s persistent call—draws us back to Him. Even when we feel alone, misunderstood, or broken, it is in those very moments of solitude and vulnerability that God meets us most powerfully. Jacob’s wrestling with God left him with a limp, a visible reminder of his encounter with the divine. In the same way, our weaknesses and wounds can become the very places where God’s grace is most evident.

We are called to be a church that welcomes people as they are, not demanding perfection before they enter, but trusting that God will do the work of transformation. Just as fish are caught before they are cleaned, so too are we invited to come to Christ with all our mess, trusting Him to make us new. Our struggles, failures, and even our sins are not wasted; God uses all things for our good and His glory.

As we partook in Holy Communion, we proclaimed the victory of Christ, who was broken and raised again, and we received the resurrection power that enables us to rise after every fall. No matter what we face, the God who called Jacob “Israel” calls us to rally our strength, to stand in the new identity He has given us, and to trust that His purpose for us will prevail. In our weakness, His strength is made perfect, and in our brokenness, His grace shines brightest.

title: Highlights l 26 October 2025 l Pastor Jeremy Govender
description:
So often, we find ourselves weighed down by the challenges and disappointments of life, feeling as though we are not qualified or worthy to receive the promises God has spoken over us. Many of us carry a sense of insecurity, believing that our past mistakes or failures have disqualified us from God’s best. Yet, the story of Israel’s journey into the Promised Land reminds us that God’s faithfulness is not dependent on our perfection, but on His power and purpose. When the Israelites finally stood on the threshold of their inheritance, they were met not with ease, but with opposition—nations bigger and stronger than themselves. This was not a sign of God’s absence, but rather a stage for His strength to be revealed.

Life rarely unfolds as simply as we hope. We expect that, after all we’ve endured, the breakthrough should come easily. But God often allows us to face “Jebusites”—those last, stubborn strongholds that seem impossible to overcome. These are not meant to defeat us, but to remind us that the victory is not by our might, but by God’s hand. The city that once mocked David and Israel, declaring they would never enter, became the very place of their greatest victory—the City of David. In the same way, the areas in our lives where the enemy seems most entrenched are often the places God intends to give us as a testimony of His power.

We must not measure our worth or our future by our failures. Like a footballer who scores one out of every six or seven shots, our lives are not defined by the misses, but by the victories God brings. God is not keeping a tally of our mistakes; He is building a highlight reel of His faithfulness in our story. The end of the story is already written—God is the author and the finisher. He knows the greatness that is still to come in your life, and He has chosen you not in spite of your failures, but because He knows what you will accomplish through Him.

So, let us shift our focus from our regrets to our highlights. Let us remember the times God brought us through, the moments He proved Himself faithful, and the victories that seemed impossible. The battle is not over, and the story is not finished. God is able to do exceedingly, abundantly more than we could ask or imagine—not just for others, but for you, personally. Walk in that confidence, knowing that your greatest victories may still be ahead.

title: If God Was Dead I 19 October 2025 I Pastor Jeremy Govender
description:
We reflected on the sobering words of Romans 1, which paint a picture of a world that lives as if God is dead - ignoring His truth, embracing wickedness, and exchanging the glory of the Creator for created things. It’s easy to point fingers at the world, but the real challenge is to examine our own hearts. Do we, who claim to know Christ, sometimes live as if He is absent or powerless? Is our faith reduced to rituals, church attendance, and outward conformity, while our hearts grow cold and distant from the Living God?

The call is to move beyond religion and into a vibrant, daily relationship with the God who is alive. God is not interested in empty traditions or superficial acts of worship. He desires to walk with us, to speak to us, and to fill us with His Spirit. The evidence of a living faith is not in how many times we show up at church, but in the fruit of our lives—our prayer, our hunger for His Word, our integrity, our forgiveness, and our hope in the face of trials.

No matter what the world says or how dark things may seem, our God is not dead. He is alive, powerful, and present. He is able to heal, restore, provide, and deliver. The same Spirit that raised Christ from the dead lives in us, empowering us to live with hope, courage, and love. Let us not settle for a dead religion, but pursue a living relationship with Jesus, so that when the world looks at us, they see evidence that our God is truly alive.
